en: The *Vyavastholikā* of Nāgabuddhi (Toh. no.
1809), the *Samājasādhanavyavasthāli* (The Stages of the Arrangement of the *Guhyasamāja* Sādhana) by Nāgabodhi.
Homage to Vajrasattva. *Derge Tanjur*, vol. NGI, folios 121r.6–131r.5. [Göttingen Xc 14/30] [21v2] *namo vajrasattvāya*.
Having paid homage to Vajrasattva, whose body is the indivisibility of the three vajras,
the systematic arrangement of the limbs of the sādhana of the *Samāja* is now proclaimed.
First, having recited the verse beginning with "abhāva," one should cause the categories of things, such as the immobile and so forth, to enter into emptiness.

Therein, having established the ground by means of the four mandalas—beginning with "one should visualize the wind-mandala situated in the center of the space-element"—one should, upon that, [visualize] a peaked palace (kūṭāgāra) by means of the syllable *bhrūṃ*. Having thus resolved through such conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one should arrange the entire wheel of deities beginning with Akṣobhya therein.

Then, having manifested oneself as Mahāvajradhara through the sequence of yoga, subsequent yoga, excessive yoga, and great yoga, and having emitted the deities of the maṇḍala by means of the union of the two organs, one should perform recitation and meditation and then dismiss them; thus the instruction on the placement [of mantras] is indicated.
Now, the *vyavastholi* [the sequence of dissolution] states the third instruction:

When, in this world, not even a single sentient being remains in the triple realm (*traidhātuka*) as it undergoes its final contraction, and only the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) persists, then, gradually, the rays of seven suns appear and, having incinerated the triple realm, reduce it to the nature of space. A practitioner of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) contemplates this meaning by reciting the verse beginning with "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, by the power of the continuous flow of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), very gentle winds begin to stir. Then, those winds increasing in strength form a wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*) above space, sixteen hundred thousand *yojanas* in depth and incalculable in circumference. Upon that wind-circle, clouds gather and rain down in streams as thick as axles; this becomes the water-circle (*apāṃ maṇḍala*). Its measurement is eleven hundred thousand and twenty thousand *yojanas* in depth.

Furthermore, those waters, being churned by the winds, become a golden earth above the waters; its measurement is three hundred thousand [yojanas] in thickness, plus twenty thousand. The circle of fire, however, is indeed contained within it.

This arising of the arrangement [of the world] is the yogins' visualization of the wind-maṇḍala situated in the midst of the space-element, and so forth; by means of the sequence of the four maṇḍalas, there is the support of the earth-portion. In this way, by means of winds produced through the power of the karma of sentient beings, gold and other substances are gathered together and formed into heaps. Thus, mountains such as Sumeru, the celestial palaces of the gods, the continents, the trees up to the Cakravāḍa range, and the shrubs and creepers come into existence.

By this much of the text, it has been stated that for those practicing the stage of generation of existence, one should first perform the meditation on emptiness as a characteristic, then prepare the site of the earth according to the sequence of the four mandalas, and upon that, construct the gabled palace (kūṭāgāra).

Then Mahāvajradhara, the Lord of Consciousness and progenitor of beings, having brought forth the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), emanates the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). This is because it is stated that "the meditation on the arising of the three vajras must be performed preceded by the accomplishment of the *ālaya*.

In this regard, there are four modes of birth (*yoni*): namely, egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), womb-born (*jarāyuja*), moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*), and spontaneously born (*upapāduka*). "Mode of birth" means birth. What is the egg-born mode of birth? It refers to those sentient beings who are born from eggs, such as swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mainas, and so forth.
What is the womb-born birth (*jarāyuja-yoni*)? It refers to those beings who are born from a placenta, such as elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, donkeys, pigs, humans, and so forth.
What is the moisture-born birth (*saṃsveda-ja-yoni*)? It refers to those beings who are born from the moisture of the elements, such as worms, insects, moths, mosquitoes, and so forth.

What is the apparitional birth (*upapāduka-yoni*)? It refers to those beings who are born all at once, complete and lacking no faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, such as gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*), the beings of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*), and so forth.

Here it is asked: since humans dwell even in the three other continents, for what reason do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas in their final existence not descend there from the sublime realm of Tuṣita? They necessarily descend here in Jambudvīpa and teach the Dharma to humans. May the Blessed One, the Teacher Vajraguru, explain the reason for this.

The Vajra Master said: "In Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru, humans possess the conditions for great enjoyment; however, they are slow-witted, dull, and live without discernment. This Jambudvīpa is the land of karma. Therefore, here the ripening of the fruits of action is seen for beings who have performed good or evil deeds—whether superior, middling, or inferior. For it is thus in this Jambudvīpa that humans are characterized by deceit, hypocrisy, pride, envy, and corrupt intentions, and are tormented by old age and disease."

Rather, they are those who understand through a mere hint, possess sharp faculties, and are of a keen disposition. Therefore, Bodhisattvas are born only in the central regions of Jambudvīpa and there they teach the Dharma.
Hence it is said:
"The first treasure is the attainment of human birth."
The gain of renunciation is the second treasure;
the gain of going forth is the third treasure;
and the gain of meditative concentration is the fourth treasure.

The *Asādhāraṇaguhyamahāyogatantra* also states: "All Buddhas of the past, future, and present, abiding in human form, attain the state of omniscient accomplishment. For this reason, the generation stage for humans is explained.

The humans of the first eon were adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha; they were corporeal yet mind-made, endowed with all major and minor limbs, unimpaired, and possessed of unimpaired faculties. Having bodies of beautiful complexion, self-luminous, moving through the sky, long-lived, nourished by joy, and embodiments of wisdom, they did not understand the illusion-like samādhi.

Not understanding this, by the power of the continuous stream of the latencies of ignorance since beginningless time, they are gradually overwhelmed by the karma and afflictions arising from their own minds. Consequently, having cast off the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), they successively take up an ordinary human existence through the continuity of afflictions. Thus, the Vajra of one's own mind, being devoid of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and failing to know its own nature, remains in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for seven days after passing away again and again from the class of sentient beings until it obtains the conditions for rebirth; this is the certainty [of the teaching].

He asked: "What is the characteristic of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? He replied: "The personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) that arises between the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*), for the purpose of reaching rebirth in another location—that is called the intermediate state.

And it possesses sharp faculties. Just as a Bodhisattva in his final existence (*caramabhavika*) enters the mother’s womb with full youth and endowed with all the marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of an omniscient one, even so does one dwelling in the intermediate state enter the mother’s womb. Furthermore, a hundred million lamps appear before him."

As it is said in the *Bhadrapāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "That man who has been born there, having cast off his [former] life, recovers divine mindfulness. He sees the gods of the six desire realms; he sees the sixteen great hells. And he sees his own body with even hands and feet, and he understands thus: 'This is my present body. As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośakārikā*: "Visible to those of the same class and to those with pure divine eyes, possessing the speed of supernatural power through karma."
Possessing all the senses, unimpeded, and irreversible, he is a consumer of odors.

By this, for those who practice the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), the perfected form of the deity is made known through the sequence of yoga and its application. Just as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in his final existence, considering that he cannot accomplish the welfare of humans through the *saṃbhogakāya*, demonstrates his entry into a womb in order to assume a *nirmāṇakāya* by way of entering the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*);

so too, one abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) assumes birth through this sequence, impelled by karma arising from the continuity of beginningless habitual tendencies of one’s own conceptualization after the passing of seven days.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: when the humans of the first eon were consuming ambrosia as food, until finally, with the consumption of solid food, coarseness and heaviness increased in their bodies and their radiance disappeared. Then, when darkness had arisen, the sun and moon appeared in the world.

Then, for the sake of demonstrating the distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), the female and male organs appeared among them, though their physical forms remained undifferentiated. As they looked at one another, by the power of their previous habitual practice, a mind of mutual passion arose. Because they then engaged in misconduct, from that time onward the distinct designation "woman" and "man" has continued to prevail in the world even to this day.

Then, due to the manifestation of three conditions, that being who is a Gandharva descends into the mother’s womb as an embryo: the mother is a maiden (kalyā) and is in her fertile period; the parents are filled with passion; and having seen their mutual union through the embrace, kissing, and other acts resulting from the empowerment of the vajra of mutual passion, and having witnessed the conjunction of the two organs, he abandons the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for the sake of grasping at sensual desire.

Like a horseman, the Mind-Vajra, presided over by consciousness, mounted upon the wind-vehicle, arrives most swiftly; having entered through the door of Vairocana in a mere instant, a moment, or a muhūrta—like a *jñānasattva* (or, according to Tanaka, a *jñānasattva* of possession)—he reaches the ground of gnosis and becomes non-dual with the gnosis of skillful means, his heart captivated by joy.

In accordance with the method of the *samādhi* for overcoming all Tathāgatas taught in the Tantras, one stimulates the seventy-two thousand channels mentioned in the *Prajñāsūtra*, and having gratified both [the male and female consorts] with the bliss of supreme joy, they become unified through the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*). Upon entering the subtle elements, through the arising of the rays of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), both are melted; having become mixed with the semen and blood, it falls into the center of the womb in the form of a drop (*bindu*).
Illuminating this point, the *Mūlasūtra* states: “He dwells within the bhagas of the vajra-women who are the heart-essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

From that, [the embryo] develops in succession. First, it takes the form of the *kalala*; from the *kalala*, the *arbuda* is born; from the *arbuda*, the *peśī* is born; and from the *peśī*, the *ghana* is born. Then, being impelled by the wind (*vāyu*), from the *ghana* there arise the five types of swellings in the form of branches and sub-branches. Thereafter, the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the sense organs, physical forms, and secondary characteristics, develop in due order.

And through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the five Tathāgatas, beginning from the stage of the seed-syllable (*bījāvasthā*), it arises in five forms (*pañcākāra*). In this regard, the *kalala* is the empowerment of Akṣobhya; the *arbuda* is that of Ratnasaṃbhava; the *peśī* is that of Amitābha; the *ghana* is that of Amoghasiddhi; and the *praśākhā* is the empowerment of Vairocana.

It also shows the fivefold form even of the great passion (*mahārakta*). Among those, the fluid (*drava*) belongs to Akṣobhya; the blood (*rakta*) belongs to Amitābha; the embryo-mass (*peśī*) belongs to Ratnasaṃbhava; the solid mass (*ghana*) belongs to Amoghasiddhi; and the mixture (*saṃmiśra*) is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vairocana.
Furthermore, there are two channels in the middle of the womb, namely on the left and the right:
one should know that the semen (*śukra*) is on the left, and the blood (*rakta*) is indeed on the right.
The merging of those two, their oneness within the *dharmadhātu*, is called "inclusion."

...by means of the internal winds born of the maturation of karma, which belong to that [being] who has attained the state of fruition within the womb in the mother’s belly. These winds, having reached the embryo, transform it and establish it facing the opening of the *dharmodaya* (the source of phenomena) within the mother’s belly.

If it is a male, it takes recourse in the mother’s right side, facing her back, and is born in a crouching position. If it is a female, then it takes recourse in the left side and faces the front of the abdomen.

Then, at the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in order to demonstrate the vajra-samādhi arising from the pledge (samaya) as taught in the Mūlasūtra. Consequently, that gandharva-being became visible to the eye of flesh. Therefore, it is said in the Mūlasūtra: "The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bodhicittavajra, was seen by all the Tathāgatas in the form of three faces.
Regarding this, it is said:
"The water element is to be known as paternal, and the fire element as maternal."
Skin, flesh, and blood are said to be derived from the mother;
sinews, marrow, bone, and semen are called derived from the father. These are declared to be the constituent parts that compose the physical body.

"Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness itself— the image consisting of the five Buddhas is said to be the aggregates and so forth. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*.

By means of this much of the text, the mantra-practitioner should generate firm conviction, thinking, "I am one who has accomplished the four yogas. Thus ends the first chapter, the establishment of the generation stage. ||o||

The instruction on the second placement; the second chapter on the instruction for the placement. || || [Then] he states the second instruction: the second chapter on the instruction for the placement. || ||
Now he states the third instruction concerning the systematic arrangement. First, the maṇḍala of the body is established:
beginning from the Brahma-thread, divided into four squares, the characteristic of the yogins' body appears like a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra).
"Bhaga is the maṇḍala," he says; "and the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is the maṇḍala";
"the body is said to be the maṇḍala"—thus is the conceptualization of the maṇḍala threefold, according to the statement in the *Samājottara*.

Regarding the causal relationship of the deities arranged according to the nature of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) within one's own body-maṇḍala thus constituted, it is said: therein, Vairocana is in the aggregate of form; Ratnasaṃbhava is in the aggregate of feeling; Amitābha is in the aggregate of perception; Amoghasiddhi is in the aggregate of mental formations; and Akṣobhya is in the aggregate of consciousness.

Therefore, it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas. Thus, because of the arrangement of the aggregates [as] Tathāgatas, the five aggregates become the causes of awakening, as stated in the *Mūlasūtra*: "Hatred, delusion, and likewise passion—these five families, consisting of wish-fulfilling jewels, are indeed the accomplishers of desire and liberation."

He explains the arrangement of the goddesses: Locanā, who delights in delusion, is the earth element; Māmakī, who delights in hatred, is the water element; Pāṇḍaravāsinī, who delights in passion, is the fire element; and Tārā, who delights in the vajra, is the air element. Illuminating this meaning, he says in the *Mūlasūtra*: "Locanā is known as earth;
Māmakī is remembered as water; Pāṇḍarā is known as fire; and Tārā is proclaimed as air."
Having understood the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of these elements (*dhātu*) as well, through the arrangement of the deities, the elements become bestowers of Buddhahood.

He describes the cause and fruit of the Bodhisattvas who are arranged in the sense-bases (*āyatana*), such as the eye and so forth. That very Blessed One is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*). Abiding in the faculty of the eye through the *Kṣitigarbha* samādhi, having analyzed the threefold form as luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he bestows the Vajra-eye faculty.
Likewise, Vajrapāṇi, abiding in the faculty of the ear, having similarly analyzed the threefold sound, bestows the Vajra-ear faculty.

Ākāśagarbha, abiding in the olfactory faculty, examines the three types of odor and bestows the adamantine olfactory faculty. Lokeśvara, abiding in the gustatory faculty, examines the three types of taste and bestows the adamantine gustatory faculty.
The Blessed Mañjuśrī, abiding in the six evolving consciousnesses, examines the three types of gnosis and bestows the superknowledge of knowing the minds of others.

The Blessed One Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, abiding in the body-faculty, causes the hindrances to vanish, condenses them together with one another, enters into birth, and brings about the vajra-body. The Blessed One Samantabhadra, abiding everywhere at the points of articulation, beholds the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) at those joints.
The Blessed One Maitreya, abiding in the nature of the sinews, binds with the sinews and causes entry into the luminosity.

That very Blessed One, appearing externally in the form of the three aspects, is Rūpavajrā because she bestows the pleasure of the eye faculty; in this same way, it should be understood for Śabdavajrā and the others as well.
For the Blessed One Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed the union of all;

as it is stated in the *Samvara*: "His enjoyment is indeed the entirety of the three realms without exception. By means of this placement of the goddesses and through the thorough knowledge of their intrinsic nature, one brings about the purification of the sense objects.

Illuminating this point, the *Mūlasūtra* says: "The vajra-spheres themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the bodhisattvas; the mantra-practitioner should constantly visualize the deity through form, sound, and so forth."
He describes the causal relationship for those who have distributed their wrath into the limbs:
Yamāntaka is on the right arm; Aparājita is on the left;
Hayagrīva is to be visualized on the face; and Amṛtakuṇḍalī is on the vajra.
One should visualize Acala on the right arm and Ṭakkirāja on the left; on the right knee, the intensely radiant Nīladaṇḍaka;
on the left knee, Mahābala; and upon the head, Uṣṇīṣavajrin.
One should contemplate Sumbharāja placed at the two ends of the feet.

These ten wrathful kings, when arrayed upon the limbs of the practitioner, emerge effortlessly from the body-maṇḍala in the form of three faces and six arms, and they threaten the hosts of obstructors in the ten directions.

Therefore, it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*: "The wrathful ones, born in the abode of hatred, are eternally intent on slaying; they are accomplished for the purpose of slaying by the practitioner who possesses the foremost qualities."
The third chapter: The Arrangement of the Body Maṇḍala. || 0 ||

The mantra-practitioner, having realized the cause and fruit of the deities arranged within the body-maṇḍala, emanates the emanation-maṇḍala from the body-maṇḍala for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others through this sequence. This is the sequence:

having mentally expanded [the visualization of] a woman of his own family, or else having taken an external woman and performed the union of the two organs according to the procedure stated in the *Sādhana*, he should produce the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) either from the bodhicitta—emanated solely by the mantra—or by the previously mentioned sequence. Then, uttering the mantra beginning with "Vajradhṛk," he should create the entire circle of deities.
He states the rule for the mantra of emission: he is called Vajradhṛk because he holds the vajra which indicates the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*).

Having purified the affliction of hatred (*dveṣakleśa*) by means of this, he returns and becomes non-dual with Mahāvajradhara; through the yoga of union (*saṃpuṭayoga*), he is established in the form of Akṣobhya within the central maṇḍala.
Thus, because he conquers the four Māras from the twelvefold wheel of Dharma, he is Jinajik.
He is called Ratnadhṛk because he holds the jewel that fulfills all hopes.
*Ā* signifies *saṃsāra*, which is "wandering" (*arova*) everywhere; he goes beyond (*liṅg*) that *saṃsāra*, thus he is Ārolik.
Wisdom has the characteristic of discernment; he holds that, thus he is Prajñādhṛk.
Delusion is Vairocana; delight in that is "delight in delusion. Hatred is Akṣobhya; delight in that is "delight in hatred.
Passion is Amitābha; delight in that is "delight in passion."
The vajra is the unerring; delight in it is vajrarati.
He whose internal womb (*garbha*) is the immovable meditative concentration (*acalitasamādhi*) even within the earth is Kṣitigarbha.

He is Vajrapāṇi because he holds the vajra, which has the nature of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*). Ākāśagarbha is he whose womb is space (*ākāśa*), which is unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna*).
By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he is the Lord of the worlds, the World-Lord (*lokeśvara*).
From the luminous meditative concentration (*prabhāsvara-samādhi*), Mañjuśrī possesses charming glory.

Because he suppresses and paralyzes the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśa*) through the power of the illusion-like meditative concentration (*māyopama-samādhi*), he is the Dispeller of All Hindrances (*sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin*).
Maitreya is so called by virtue of his power of focusing on loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward beings such as those without feet, those with two feet, and those with four feet.
Samantabhadra means "all-pervading," "excellent," or "auspicious.

That by which something is manifested or reflected is *rūpa* (form). That which is sounded is *śabda* (sound). That which is smelled is *gandha* (odor). That which is tasted is *rasa* (taste). That which is touched is *sparśa* (tangible object). Through the presence of the word "vajra," he describes the purification of form and the other sense objects by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Yama is hell; because that Blessed One destroys it through the samādhi of great wrath, he is Yamāntakṛt. Because he brings an end to bonds through wisdom, he is Prajñāntakṛt.
Because he brings an end to those with impure passion by means of the analogy of the lotus, he is Padmāntakṛt.

The four Māras are the obstacles; because that Blessed One brings them to an end through the meditative absorption of Great Wrath, he is Vighnāntakṛt (Obstacle-Ender). Because he brings about the realization of the eight worldly concerns—which constantly agitate the hearts of beings—through the diamond-like meditative absorption, he is Acala (Immovable). *Ṭakki* means desire; because he rules, shines, and is purified, he is Ṭakkirāja (King Ṭakki).
He is Nīladaṇḍa because he wields the blue staff, which is the punishment and restraint for the sins of sentient beings.
He is Mahābala because, through the power of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he crushes the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of sentient beings.
He is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin because he bestows the knowledge that has emerged from the three realms (*traidhātuka*) upon sentient beings.
Having summoned the hosts of obstructors from the ten directions, King Nisumbha [performs] the ritual of pinning and the ritual of crushing. ||o||

These thirty-two deities, appearing with three faces and six arms, holding various insignia and mudrās in their hands, emerged effortlessly from the body-maṇḍala of the practitioner—either from the *bodhicitta* or from a single emanation of mantra—in order to increase the accumulation of merit. Having purified the obscurations of the afflictions and so forth of sentient beings who engage in passion, hatred, delusion, and the like, by means of their respective meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), they returned and sat upon their individual seats.

The vajra, wheel, jewel, lotus, sword, and bell are said to be the six symbols of the Tathāgatas respectively; these very same [symbols] are held in the form of weapons. They are distinguished by differences in color according to the specific ritual actions, such as pacification (śānti) or enrichment (puṣṭi).
Because it is endowed with all jewels, [the symbol] is the color of sapphire (indranīla).

Elucidating this very maṇḍala of emanation (*utsargamaṇḍala*), the *Mūlasūtra* states: "Then indeed, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya empowered the stainless Great Samaya-maṇḍala within the wombs (*bhaga*) of all the Tathāgatas’ consorts. It was transparent and of that very nature, appearing in various forms on all sides; it was filled with clouds of Buddhas and agitated by a dense mass of sparks. Endowed with the maṇḍalas of transparency and so forth, it is the city of all the Tathāgatas. It is asked: "If there is no hand-seal (*hastamudrā*) in this tantra, how is the form of the deity, which is sealed by the four seals (*caturmudrā*), brought to completion?"

He said: The Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is the female deity whose form serves as the basis adorned with the ornaments of all the qualities of a Buddha without exception; the Pledge Seal (samayamudrā) is the woman; the Dharma Seal (dharmamudrā) is the very syllables of the mantra; and the Action Seal (karmamudrā) is the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world.
He asked: "Why is it that here the form of three faces is seen, whereas in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other tantras of both classes, the single face is established?
He replied: "The Blessed One himself stated the reason in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇavyākhyātantra*:
'This is the Great Reality (Mahātattva), which indeed consists of both the external and the internal.'"
The non-dual state is declared to be the conceptualization of both reality [and its opposite].
The little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger,
the forefinger, and likewise the thumb are proclaimed to correspond in number to form and the other [sensory objects] on the left hand.
Because these are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are characterized by the discernment of wisdom;
this is declared to be the Dharmakāya, designated as suchness and non-duality.
The Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Ratna, Amitābha, Amogha,
and Vairocana are likewise positioned with their right hands starting from the little finger.
The Sangha is one for each of the two; thus, this is the triad of refuges.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Sangha—though they are one, they constitute three conceptualizations.
Vajrasattva, the supreme state of wisdom and means, is bound with one another;
by merely forming the añjali gesture, one brings all the Buddhas together.
He is the triple refuge, the triple reality, the triple body, and the triple liberation;
he is the triple face, the three syllables, the triple deity, and likewise the one who dwells within the three realms.

He is the three paths, the three samayas, the supreme, the triad, and the triple mandala; he is the triple yoga, the triple path, and as many as are enjoined by the kalpas. In the worlds of supplication and salutation, there is the act of prayer.
That which stands from your joined palms shall be a gratification for the Perfectly Awakened One.
"Those sentient beings would be Buddhas by virtue of the non-dual reality of suchness;
all Buddhas are established through the yoga of abiding in the non-abiding.

He asked: "In this *Guhyasamāja*, various arrangements of the deities of the maṇḍala are practiced according to the preferences of different teachers in the world. How, then, can practitioners become free from doubt?"

[He said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāsattva! I shall explain this to you through both reasoning and scripture. Just as there is the arrangement of deities by way of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth within the body-maṇḍala, so too must there be an arrangement of deities within the abandonment-maṇḍala (*utsargamaṇḍala*). Nevertheless, the complete arrangement of deities does not exist in the *Mūlasūtra*. However, it was not taught by the Blessed One that the arrangement of the maṇḍala should be performed in its entirety in a single location, lest it lead to the improper practice of the master."
It is demonstrated in one place in the explanatory tantra, the *Śrīvajramālā*. That is now introduced:
"Listen, O Great Being, do not recall this with a distracted mind. Within this body of the Vajrācārya, the sequence of the Victorious Ones abiding in the body [is present]."
First, he is established as the aggregate of form by means of the body-vajra;
he is established as the aggregate of sensation by means of the passion-vajra.
The Blessed One is established as the aggregate of perception by means of the speech-vajra;
he is established as the aggregate of mental formations by means of the vajra of all worship.
By means of the mind-vajra, that Blessed One, although abiding in the aggregate of consciousness, [is present];
and the earth element consisting of flesh and so forth is the Blessed Lady Locanā, who is likewise established there.
The water element consisting of blood and so forth is the Blessed Lady Māmakī;
the fire element consisting of heat and so forth is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
The goddess Tārā is situated as the impelling wind-element;
likewise, the Tathāgata Kṣitigarbha is the sense-organ of his two eyes.
The faculty of his two ears is the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi;
the faculty situated in his nose is the Tathāgata Gaganagañja.
The faculty abiding in the tongue is the Tathāgata Lokeśvara;
the faculty abiding in the mind is the Tathāgata Mañjughoṣa.
This body, known as a physical mass, consists of the four elements;
within it dwells the Tathāgata Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
The Tathāgata Samantabhadra is all the joints of the body;
the Tathāgata Maitreya is all the sinews of the body.
At the base of the right arm is the Tathāgata Yamāntaka;
at the base of the left arm is the Tathāgata Aparājita;
and upon the lotus-face resides the Tathāgata Hayagrīva.
The Tathāgata Amṛtakuṇḍalī abides in the secret region.
That Tathāgata Acala stands upon the right arm; the Tathāgata Ṭakkirāja stands upon the left arm;
and the Tathāgata Nīladaṇḍa stands upon the right knee.
The Tathāgata Mahābala should stand upon the left knee;
the Tathāgata Cakravartin should stand upon the crown of his own head;
and the Tathāgata Sumbharāja should stand beneath his feet.

All the Tathāgatas abide within this entire body; thus is described the Body Maṇḍala, which is the physical form of the Vajrācārya. All these perfectly awakened Buddhas are gathered together as the Buddha-body.
The Vajra-holder leads those who teach the conditioned toward nirvāṇa.
O Blessed One, may you quickly enter nirvāṇa; may your wholesome qualities reach full maturity.
Therefore, all the Victors are empowered within the body of the Vajra-Guru.
In a future time, O Mahāsattva Amoghadarśaka, listen!
Beginners among sentient beings must serve their guru with great diligence.
Likewise, together with Amoghadarśin, the highly renowned Bodhisattvas—
Satisfied, joyful, and thrilled, they bowed down with tears falling.

He said: "One should place all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who have abandoned all afflictions and attained the qualities of a Buddha such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses—within this ordinary body. [This is a contradictory statement.]

[He asked: "Just as when a person is in the state of a physical substance (*dravyāvasthā*), even though phlegm is not actually present, they are called 'phlegmatic' (*śleṣmika*); yet in the state of an image (*pratimāvasthā*), worship is performed [for that same person]. Likewise, the ordinary body and [the afflictions] such as passion, hatred, and delusion—which in their prior state are causes of *saṃsāra*—become, after the thorough knowledge of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), causes for the accomplishment of true gnosis (*samyagjñāna*) once they are purified. Thus, there is no fault. And so it has been said:
'Having taken hold of this impure image...'"
One fashions an image of the Jina-jewel, priceless; take up that which is exceedingly penetrable, well-firm, and born of the essence— known as the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
And so it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:

"Kāśyapa, just as all seeds sprout upon the earth when it is prepared for cultivation, even so, Kāśyapa, the Buddha-qualities of a bodhisattva sprout within the world when it is strewn with the accumulation of afflictions.
It is also said in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa-mahāyoga-tantra*:
To the illustrious Vajrapāṇi, who knew the reality of the meaning of subtle yoga,
he spoke of the subtle [teaching] after meditating through the non-dual yoga of the world.
They speak, according to their respective capacities, of this fivefold awakening— which is for the sake of people who have not yet reached it— within this *Dharmasaṅgīti*.
For these aggregates would indeed be Buddhas, arising as conditions for the sake of enlightenment;
they too are declared to be Tathāgatas by virtue of their union with non-dual suchness.
The Fourth Chapter: The Arrangement of the Mandala of Emission.
Now, the introductory statement for the demonstration of the arrangement of the ultimate reality mandala (*paramārthamaṇḍala*) is introduced from the Root Sūtra:
"From the commitment (*samaya*), one should emit semen; one should drink it according to the ritual rule, desiring the fruit."

"One should slay the array of the Tathāgatas; thus one will most certainly attain accomplishment. This is the summary. As for its detailed exposition, it is taught in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*, the Explanatory Tantra of this [work], in the seventh chapter:
"Vipaśyanā is the seeing of internal phenomena such as form and so forth."
By visualizing Akṣobhya and the others in their respective order, one becomes composed (*samatha*).
The lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of these two is designated as suchness (*tathatā*) and peace (*śānta*).
Thus, within the maṇḍala of suchness, the yogin should cause all the Buddhas to enter.
Its further explanation is as follows; it is set forth in the *Vajramālā-mahāyoga-tantra*, which is now introduced:
The mirror-like [wisdom] resides in the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); it is the earth element and the eye faculty.
Form attains accumulation, conjoined with the wrathful deity Maitreya.

The equality of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the water element (*ab-dhātu*), the faculty of hearing, and sound; it proceeds toward accumulation, endowed with the two types of anger.
And having examined perception (*saṃjñā*), fire is the faculty of the nose.
And smell goes to its accumulation, accompanied by two types of anger;
the formative forces (saṃskāra) are the performance of duties, wind is the sense of taste,
and taste goes to its accumulation, accompanied by two types of anger.
Above and below, conjoined with the wrathful deities and appearing as the primordial nature,
it enters the aggregate of consciousness, and consciousness itself becomes luminous clarity.
Together with nirvāṇa, all is empty; this is declared to be the dharmakāya.
And for the sake of strengthening [this realization], one should recite this mantra:
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of emptiness.

He states the third instruction concerning the systematic arrangement: "When the luminosity has entered the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the wise one should perceive its characteristics. All bodily forms wither; the limbs become soft and the members become flaccid.
When the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) has departed, there is a state of dimness;
when it has gone into the earth element (bhūdhātu), there is emaciation of the entire body."
When the faculty of sight has gone [to its object], a transformation of the eye occurs; it contracts.
When it has gone to the object of form, there arises a discoloration of one’s own body and a state of rigidity.

Thus, throughout beginningless saṃsāra, for beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, and so forth—those belonging to the Vairocana family, abiding in the body-maṇḍala, enter the ultimate maṇḍala by a gradual process that is momentarily slow.
For those who are situated in the constituent parts have no fixed arrangement therein; nevertheless, they enter into ultimate truth by means of a sequence.

Thus, the wise one should observe the characteristic of the time of entering ultimate truth within the deity of the second Jewel Family: when dissolved in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), bodily feelings such as the dispositions of wind, bile, and phlegm are no longer experienced;
and when dissolved in the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), one does not remember the three types of mental feeling.
When the water element has dissolved within one's own body, the sweat, urine, blood, semen, and so forth dry up.
When the auditory faculty has dissolved, the internal sound within one's own body is not heard;
when the object of sound has dissolved, one does not hear sound within one's own body.
This is the second entry into the deity of the Jewel Family.
In the third [moment], at the time of the entry of the deities of the Lotus Family, the wise one should observe the characteristic:
when the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has dissolved, he does not remember sentient beings such as bipeds;
when the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) has dissolved, he does not remember any perceptions of the world, such as mother, son, or kinsmen.
When the fire element (*tejodhātu*) has dissolved, all bodily heat perishes.
When the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) has dissolved, breathing becomes faint and one gasps for breath;
the object of smell within one's own body is no longer perceived.
The entry into the family deity of the Lotus family.
The wise one should perceive the characteristic of entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) through the deities of the fourth action-family.
When the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) has dissolved therein, all bodily activity ceases to function.
When the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) has dissolved, one no longer remembers the activities and operations of external worldly existence.
When the wind element has dissolved, the ten winds, beginning with prāṇa, are dispersed from their own locations.
When the tongue faculty has dissolved, the tongue becomes thick, short, and blue at its base.
When the object of taste has dissolved, the six tastes are no longer experienced.
The entry into the deity of the fourth action-family.
The remainder, the manifestation of the primordial nature (*prakṛtyābhāsa*), which is the wisdom of Mañjuśrī, is known through the second stage.

Abiding by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) together with the sequence of the vajra-recitation, one effects the withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) into the body during the state of the *piṇḍa* (the mass) through the sequence of the wind (*anila*). At that time, the mantra "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness" becomes directly realized.
He said: "May the Blessed One, the Vajra Teacher, explain the meaning of the mantra."
The Vajra-Guru said: "It was taught by the Blessed One himself in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*). Then all the Tathāgatas, established in the subtle yoga, [spoke]:
'Oṃ'—this is joined as one; the second is 'emptiness' (*śūnyatā*)."
The third is simply "knowledge," and the fourth is designated as "vajra.
The sixth is proclaimed as "I am the one whose nature is the self of phenomena" (*svabhāvātmaka*).
Thus has the group of six Tathāgatas been described for the supreme person.
"Oṃ śūnyatā"—this pair is the beginning; the second is the *vajra* of gnosis (*jñāna*).
"I am of the nature of intrinsic being" (*svabhāvātmakaḥ*)—here, the threefold *tāra* is conceived. These three become one, which is designated as the "Perfectly Correct" (*samyak*).
A certain man, a holder of the other vajra and vajra, having been summoned by the three... [omitted], there should be the invocation, the dismissal, and likewise the stabilization.
The invocation is performed through a swift entry.
The *Caturthavyavasthāna* composed by the accomplished master Nāgabuddhi is hereby complete.
